artworks.title: Habitat
artworks.description: Habitats provide homes for all living things, from the tiniest ant to the tallest tree. This exhibition explores the critical need for varied habitats, how interconnected and fragile they are, and what we can do to protect them. The experience showcases the unique habitats throughout the gardens and landscapes of Museum grounds. Plants, animals and other organisms have adapted to each other and their habitats over time, creating a delicate ecological balance. This balance faces many threats, including pollution, deforestation and climate change, but humans can protect habitats for the future by learning to be better stewards of the environment. The exhibit invites visitors to learn more about topics related to habitats, their importance to life and what people can do to help preserve them. Sections on topics such as fungi, dead wood, nests and insects explore the critical role that many organisms play in creating and sustaining habitats, and how people can best protect them. Habitat was developed by Smithsonian Gardens and is made available by the Smithsonian Institution Traveling Exhibition Service. artworks.title: Dr. Seuss National Memorial Sculpture Garden
artworks.description: Celebrate the imagination of Dr. Seuss in the Dr. Seuss National Memorial Sculpture Garden, a whimsical outdoor experience honoring Springfield native Theodor Seuss Geisel in the city where his story began. Since opening in 2002, the garden has welcomed millions of visitors who come to explore, play, and share memorable moments alongside beloved Seuss characters brought to life in bronze. Created by sculptor Lark Grey Dimond-Cates, Geisel’s stepdaughter, the charming sculptures capture the creativity, humor, and heart that made Dr. Seuss one of the world’s most treasured storytellers. From larger-than-life characters to familiar favorites, the garden invites visitors of all ages to imagine, discover, and celebrate the enduring legacy of Dr. Seuss. Learn more about the artistry behind the sculptures in the gallery dedicated to their creation inside the Amazing World of Dr. Seuss Museum. The Grinch and Max

artworks.title: Living Waters: From Oceans to Valleys
artworks.description: Our popular live animal center has evolved! Through living exhibits, explore habitats from around the world and right in our own neighborhood. Get up close with beloved inhabitants like the wood turtle and poison dart frogs and meet new aquatic animals from Africa and South America, with new large interactives and a wall of fish fossils for a deeper experience. This permanent exhibit has been made possible through a federal earmark from The Offices of Senators Elizabeth Warren and Ed Markey and The National Institute of Standards and Technology. Massachusetts Eastern Box Turtle Terrarium Biome: Deciduous Forest Region: Northeastern United States Eastern Box Turtles (Terrapene carolina carolina) are native to the Eastern North America with a range from Maine to Georgia. Eastern box turtle habitat includes open woodlands, meadows, wetlands, and nearby stream and river banks. Eastern box turtles eat both plants and animals. Their diets include insects, worms, fruits, vegetables, mushrooms, and seeds. Connecticut River Watershed Aquarium Biome: Freshwater River within Deciduous Forest Region: Northeastern United States Pumpkinseed Sunfish (Lepomis gibbosus) are native to Eastern North America living in ponds, lakes, streams, and slow-moving parts of rivers. Pumpkinseeds feed on insects, snails, and crustaceans, amphibians, and small fishes. artworks.title: R.E. Phelon African Hall
artworks.description: Journey across the landscapes of Africa in the R.E. Phelon African Hall, where immersive exhibits explore the continent’s remarkable wildlife, rich cultural traditions, and lasting impact on the world. Follow the winding path through realistic habitats filled with iconic animals, including a towering African bush elephant, giraffe, rhinoceros, zebra, leopard, chimpanzee, warthog, and a variety of antelope. As the sounds of birds and wildlife fill the hall, you’ll feel transported to the African plains. Along the way, discover exhibits that explore human evolution and Africa’s central role in our shared history. On the upper level, explore authentic artifacts from diverse African cultures, learn about life in modern Africa, and discover the stories of prominent African Americans from Springfield. Interactive experiences, including touchable animal hides and tracks, along with multimedia presentations, encourage visitors of all ages to engage their senses and deepen their understanding of Africa’s natural and cultural heritage. artworks.title: Dinosaur Hall
artworks.description: Travel back millions of years and come face-to-face with some of Earth’s most extraordinary creatures in Dinosaur Hall. Towering overhead is a life-sized Tyrannosaurus rex, while a full-sized Stegosaurus skeleton and a replica of Coelophysis—an early dinosaur that once roamed the Connecticut River Valley nearly 200 million years ago—bring the prehistoric world to life. There’s plenty to explore beyond the skeletons. Touch real dinosaur track fossils, climb into the cast of a giant sauropod footprint, and discover how dinosaurs lived, evolved, and eventually disappeared through interactive exhibits and engaging displays. Surrounded by lush prehistoric scenery, colorful graphics, and a geologic timeline that puts Earth’s history into perspective, Dinosaur Hall offers an exciting experience for curious visitors of all ages.

artworks.title: Dinosaurs Still Live: The Story of Archosaurs
artworks.description: This bilingual exhibition invites visitors of all ages to explore the surprising connections between dinosaurs, birds, crocodilians, and pterosaurs. Through immersive environments, hands-on discovery, and engaging storytelling, the gallery reveals how these remarkable animals are linked across millions of years of evolution. Archosaurs are the group of animals that includes all living birds and crocodiles—as well as their extinct relatives such as non-avian dinosaurs, flying pterosaurs, and other ancient reptiles that once ruled land, sea, and sky. Scientists define archosaurs as all descendants of the most recent common ancestor shared by today’s birds and crocodiles. In other words, birds are living dinosaurs—and their story is still unfolding. Your journey through the exhibition is guided by four lively characters, each highlighting a chapter in the archosaur story: Hoot, Keeper of the Flock explores modern birds as living dinosaurs, with rotating displays of birds alongside their nests and eggs. Spike, Your Prehistoric Pal leads visitors through feathered dinosaurs and the evolutionary origins of flight, featuring sculpted models and tactile learning experiences. Snap, King of the Crocs showcases powerful crocodilians—from the massive prehistoric Sarcosuchus to today’s American alligator—through climbable sculptures, skull replicas, and dramatic size comparisons. Breezy, Queen of the Skies brings the age of pterosaurs to life, with full-scale silhouettes of Quetzalcoatlus

artworks.title: Springfield Science Museum
artworks.description: Discover the wonders of science, nature, and the universe at the Springfield Science Museum. For more than 160 years, the Museum has inspired curiosity through engaging exhibits, fascinating collections, and opportunities to explore the world around us—from the creatures that share our planet to the cultures that shape our stories and the mysteries of space. Explore natural history, anthropology, and physical science through experiences designed to spark questions and encourage discovery. Then journey beyond Earth at the Seymour Planetarium, home to the historic Korkosz Starball, the oldest operating star projector in the United States. Whether you’re uncovering ancient discoveries, investigating scientific phenomena, or gazing at distant galaxies, the Springfield Science Museum invites you to explore, learn, and imagine what’s possible. artworks.title: Spark!Lab
artworks.description: Imagine, build, test, and invent in Spark!Lab, a hands-on maker space where creativity takes center stage. Designed for children, families, and curious minds of all ages, Spark!Lab invites visitors to experiment, solve challenges, and bring their ideas to life through open-ended exploration. Unlike traditional craft activities, there are no step-by-step instructions or “right” answers. Instead, you’ll tackle real-world problems, brainstorm creative solutions, and discover what it takes to think like an inventor. Along the way, you’ll learn about groundbreaking inventions and innovators from American history while exploring the ideas and technologies shaping our world today. Whether you’re designing, building, testing, or reimagining something entirely new, every visit to Spark!Lab is a chance to create, collaborate, and see where your imagination can take you. Project Supporters Beveridge Family Foundation Community Foundation of Western Massachusetts Eversource Hologic, Inc. Irene E. & George A. Davis Foundation Donald and Francine Pratt Originally opened at the Smithsonian’s National Museum of American History in 2008, Spark!Lab is the flagship educational initiative of the Lemelson Center for the Study of Invention and Innovation.

artworks.title: Seymour Planetarium
artworks.description: Sit back and experience the wonders of the night sky with expert astronomers and educators. Be prepared to open your eyes to a whole new world—or worlds! The Seymour Planetarium is home to historically significant astronomy education tools as well as modern digital presentations. The Korkosz projector is a remarkable example of Springfield ingenuity. Still used in our planetarium presentation, this Springfield-made “star ball” is the oldest operating American-made projector in the world. A new full-dome video system using Zeiss Velvet projectors covers the dome with images and video, creating immersive experiences in Astronomy and Earth Science. These projectors are the only projectors in the world that have a pure black background, enhancing the beauty of our historic Korkosz projector’s optical star field. artworks.title: Earth Hall
artworks.description: Discover the incredible beauty and power of our planet in Earth Hall, where dazzling minerals, ancient rocks, and even a meteorite tell the story of Earth’s dynamic history. Marvel at brilliant crystals and rare mineral specimens from around the world, including the renowned Schortmann Collection, assembled by brothers Alvin and Raymond Schortmann from some of the world’s most celebrated mineral localities. Many of the specimens on display have been part of the Springfield Science Museum’s collection since the 1880s. As you explore, you’ll encounter glowing fluorescent minerals, an enormous amethyst geode, Massachusetts’ official state mineral—Babingtonite—and fascinating specimens from local quarries in Westfield and West Springfield. See a massive piece of Longmeadow brownstone, stand before a 290-pound meteorite discovered near Arizona’s famous Meteor Crater, and uncover the stories behind the rocks and minerals that have shaped our planet for billions of years.

artworks.title: Japanese Arms & Armor
artworks.description: For more than a century, the Japanese Arms and Armor Gallery has captured the imagination of visitors of all ages with its extraordinary samurai armor, intricate craftsmanship, and stories of honor and tradition. George Walter Vincent Smith’s collection of nearly 500 examples of Japanese arms and armor is among the most extensive of its kind and represents centuries of artistry and innovation. Acquired between 1888 and 1901, the collection includes samurai swords, blades, armor, helmets, pole arms, firearms, horse trappings, ceremonial objects, and decorative works created by master artisans. Some swords feature elegantly simple steel blades, while others showcase elaborate fittings, lacquered scabbards, and intricate metalwork. Highlights include six complete suits of armor, including a 16th-century suit belonging to the Daimyo of Arima and signed by members of the renowned Miochin armorer family. Beyond weapons and armor, the gallery reveals the artistry and symbolism of Japanese craftsmanship through objects such as a detailed silver incense burner and an elaborate Shinto wheel shrine, created over 15 years by generations of artisans. Each object tells a story of tradition, skill, and the remarkable creativity of the people who made and used them.

artworks.title: Tiffany Stained Glass Windows
artworks.description: Among the most treasured features of the George Walter Vincent Smith Art Museum are its original Tiffany stained glass windows, installed when the museum was completed in 1895. Created by the Tiffany Glass Company of New York City, these rare windows are among the few known examples of Tiffany work designed specifically for a museum building. The windows represent an important moment in the career of Louis Comfort Tiffany, who began expanding beyond religious subjects in the 1890s to create works inspired by art, literature, and culture. In the Japanese Arms and Armor Gallery, windows honor renowned writers including Goethe and Molière, while those in the lobby celebrate the museum’s original disciplines of art, science, and literature. Additional windows feature symbols connected to the history of books and printing. Designed as an integral part of George Walter Vincent Smith’s vision for the museum, the windows reflect the elegance and creativity of the Aesthetic Movement in American art. Following a careful restoration, completed in 2018, these extraordinary works of glass continue to illuminate the building and inspire visitors with their craftsmanship, color, and history. Tiffany window restoration was completed with generous funding from the Institute of Museum and Library Services, as well as support from a grant from the Springfield Cultural Council, a local agency supported by the Massachusetts Cultural Council.

artworks.title: The Grand Tour: George and Belle Smith Collect in Italy
artworks.description: In 1882, George and Belle Smith embarked on a European journey to expand their remarkable art collection. Originally planned as a two-year exploration, their travels continued for nearly four years as they immersed themselves in the art, culture, and history of Europe. The couple spent more than two years living in Venice, Italy, where they acquired many of the paintings featured in this gallery and the museum lobby. These works showcase the beauty of Venetian life and the talent of 19th-century Italian artists, including Noè Bordignon, Raffaele Mainella, Pietro Pajetta, Pasquale Ruggiero, and Ettore Tito.

artworks.title: Plaster Cast Gallery
artworks.description: In the late 19th century, American art museums were beginning to take shape, and plaster casts offered communities a way to experience some of the world’s greatest works of art without traveling overseas. These carefully crafted replicas allowed visitors to study celebrated Greek, Roman, and Renaissance sculptures and helped make art education accessible to a wider audience. Shortly after the George Walter Vincent Smith Art Museum opened, Springfield residents gained access to their own remarkable collection of plaster casts, thanks in part to support from the estate of industrialist Horace Smith. Acquired from renowned makers in Europe and the United States, the collection included reproductions of masterpieces by artists such as Donatello and Michelangelo, as well as iconic ancient sculptures like the Venus de Milo and Laocoön Group. Over time, changing attitudes toward museum collections led many institutions to remove or discard their casts. Springfield’s collection was preserved and restored, and today the George Walter Vincent Smith Art Museum is home to one of the largest collections of publicly displayed plaster casts in New England. More than historical reproductions, these sculptures tell the story of how generations of artists, students, and visitors have learned from and been inspired by great works of art. Explore the gallery to discover the artists, myths, and masterpieces behind these fascinating casts. Image above: Tomb of Lorenzo de’ Medici with Dawn and Dusk

artworks.title: Tara Sellios | Ask Now the Beasts
artworks.description: This companion exhibition to Visions of the Supernatural unveils the artist’s otherworldly vision through meticulously composed large-scale still-life photographs. Drawing on art history, symbolism, mysticism, spiritualism, and natural history, Sellios creates contemporary allegories of suffering and transcendence. Her highly detailed images feature animal skeletons, swarming insects, and dried flowers that balance the grotesque and the beautiful, inviting viewers to reflect on the complexities of religious beliefs, enduring parables, and their relevance to the human condition. Sellios’ work is deeply informed by her strict Christian upbringing and her fascination with the dramatic symbolism of religious iconography, Dutch vanitas paintings, and the fantastical visions of artists like Hieronymus Bosch. Each image is the result of a rigorous, multidisciplinary process that melds drawing, painting, and sculpture with large format photography. With Ask Now the Beasts, Sellios turns a feast’s culmination into a meditation on endings and beginnings, where devastation and hope, darkness and light, life and decay coexist. Based in the Boston area, Tara Sellios is known for her innovative work in photography that explores the carnal nature of life and human experience. She holds a BFA in Photography and Art History from the Art Institute of Boston at Lesley University and has exhibited her work in numerous solo and group exhibitions nationally and abroad. artworks.title: Visions of the Supernatural
artworks.description: Celebrate the reopening of the George Walter Vincent Smith Art Museum with Visions of the Supernatural, an immersive exhibition that reveals the museum’s remarkable collection of mysterious treasures while exploring our enduring fascination with spirits, ghosts, magic, and the unexplained. For centuries, people have sought to unlock the secrets of the afterlife. During the Victorian era, the Spiritualist movement captivated millions, offering grieving families hope that communication with the dead was possible through séances, mediums, spirit photography, automatic writing, and other paranormal practices. Drawing from the extraordinary collections, of the Springfield Museums Visions of the Supernatural examines the beliefs, rituals, objects, and cultural phenomena that shaped this remarkable chapter in history. Throughout the museum, visitors are invited to step into the world of the supernatural through engaging hands-on experiences. Try your hand at automatic writing, consult Ouija boards, gaze into crystal balls, discover the symbolic meanings of gemstones and crystals, read Tarot cards in a recreated Victorian parlor, and encounter animals, strange creatures and objects long associated with supernatural beliefs—if you dare. Blending history, mystery, art, and folklore, Visions of the Supernatural transforms the George Walter Vincent Smith Art Museum into an unforgettable journey through the strange, the mystical, and the unknown. artworks.title: American Paintings Salon
artworks.description: George Walter Vincent Smith was a passionate collector of American art, often acquiring paintings directly from the artists who created them. This gallery showcases works from Smith’s original collection alongside later additions, presented in the style of the grand Painting Salons popular during the Victorian era. In 1878, Smith organized an exhibition of 51 paintings in Springfield with the goal of “raising the cultural sights” of Western Massachusetts residents. Over the following decades, he continued to share art with the community while building a collection focused on landscapes and scenes of everyday life, including works by artists associated with the Hudson River School and American genre painting. The American Paintings Salon features works by celebrated artists including Albert Bierstadt, Thomas Cole, George Inness, John Frederick Kensett, and many others. Preserved largely as Smith assembled it, the collection offers a fascinating window into the artistic tastes, values, and cultural interests of 19th-century America.
artworks.placeNote: Where the museum’s floor map puts it.

artworks.title: Chinese Cloisonné
artworks.description: For 30 years, George Walter Vincent and Belle Townsley Smith built an extraordinary collection of Chinese cloisonné, drawn to the artistry, craftsmanship, and symbolism of these remarkable decorative objects. Although the Smiths never traveled to China, their appreciation for Chinese culture and decorative arts shaped one of the finest collections in their museum. Cloisonné is created through a meticulous process in which delicate bronze wires form intricate designs on a metal surface, creating compartments that are filled with colorful enamel and repeatedly fired in a kiln. The skill and patience required to create each piece resulted in objects of exceptional beauty and detail. The Smiths’ collection includes examples from the Ming dynasty, considered the golden age of cloisonné, as well as later works from the Qing dynasty. The gallery features a wide range of objects, including vases, dishes, incense burners, and ceremonial pieces. Among the highlights is a magnificent vase decorated with gilt bronze dragons surrounded by deep blue enamel, rich with symbolism representing wisdom, strength, and immortality. Another unusual piece, a colorful elephant carrying a vase, conveys wishes for peace and hope through traditional Chinese wordplay. Today, the Cloisonné Gallery remains true to the Smiths’ original vision, with many objects displayed in their historic late 19th-century cases and a wall color inspired by the gallery’s original design. artworks.title: Hasbro Games Art Discovery Center
artworks.description: The Art Discovery Center is a hands-on creative space where visitors of all ages can explore, imagine, and make connections with the art around them. Try a craft project, dress up in a costume, create a puppet, enjoy a story, or participate in an artist demonstration or special activity. Inspired by the George Walter Vincent Smith Art Museum’s renowned Asian art collections, the gallery is filled with vibrant colors, intricate designs, and murals featuring samurai warriors, Chinese Zodiac animals, Buddhist figures, Asian symbols, and scenes from Japanese woodblock prints. These details reflect the museum’s collections of Chinese cloisonné, Japanese arms and armor, ceramics, ivory carvings, and other decorative arts. Families can discover the meaning behind Asian symbols, explore their own Chinese horoscope, try on costumes and armor, play interactive gallery games, and create their own works of art. The Art Discovery Center invites visitors to experience creativity and culture through hands-on discovery. artworks.title: Blake Court
artworks.description: Blake Court is the grand centerpiece of the D’Amour Museum of Fine Arts, featuring soaring ceilings, a dramatic second-floor colonnade, and one of the most extraordinary works in American art. At the heart of the gallery is The Historical Monument of the American Republic by Erastus Salisbury Field—a monumental, nearly 9-by-13-foot painting that the artist spent more than 20 years creating between 1867 and 1888. Rich with symbolism, the masterpiece tells the story of the early United States through a series of imaginative architectural towers. Surrounding this iconic work are additional paintings by Field and other leading 19th-century American artists. Explore breathtaking landscapes by Hudson River School painters Frederic Church, Albert Bierstadt, and Alfred Bricher, alongside vibrant still lifes by Severin Roesen and Springfield artist J.J. LaValley. Together, these works celebrate the beauty, ambition, and imagination that defined American art during a transformative century.

artworks.title: Legacies of Surrealism: Works from the Museo de Arte de Ponce
artworks.description: This exhibition, generously loaned from the Museo de Arte de Ponce in Puerto Rico, highlights painters working throughout Latin America and exemplifies the deep influence of Surrealism in the region. Although created in the latter half of the 20th century, these works emphasize thematic and stylistic features that first appeared in the region during the 1930s and developed over the following decades. Through their exploration of the unconscious mind, they give form to dreamlike landscapes, ominous creature-like entities, and strange, non-representational organic shapes that seem inspired by nature. Generously lent by Museo de Arte de Ponce as part of Art Bridges’ Partner Loan Network. Exhibition sponsored locally by Connecticut Public. artworks.title: Michele & Donald D’Amour Museum of Fine Arts
artworks.description: Discover centuries of artistic achievement at the Michele and Donald D’Amour Museum of Fine Arts. Housed in a beautiful Art Deco building, the museum showcases an outstanding collection of American and European paintings, sculpture, prints, and watercolors, alongside Japanese woodblock prints and an impressive array of furniture, textiles, glass, ceramics, and metalwork. Highlights include exceptional French, Dutch, and Italian works, as well as one of the nation’s largest collections of Currier & Ives lithographs. From iconic masterpieces to hidden treasures, every gallery invites visitors to explore the stories, cultures, and creativity that have shaped the world of art. artworks.title: The Carol and Noel Leary Gallery of Impressionist Art
artworks.description: Experience the color, light, and innovation of the French Impressionists in one of the D’Amour Museum of Fine Arts’ most beloved galleries. Featuring masterpieces created between 1870 and 1900, this collection showcases the artists who transformed the art world by capturing everyday moments with vibrant color, visible brushstrokes, and the fleeting effects of light. The movement took its name from Claude Monet’s Impression: Sunrise, a painting whose bold style challenged the artistic conventions of its day. Though critics initially dismissed these revolutionary works, Impressionism has since become one of the most celebrated movements in art history. At the heart of the gallery is Monet’s Grainstack, accompanied by Edgar Degas’ Rehearsal Before the Ballet, Paul Gauguin’s Seascape at Brittany, Pierre-Auguste Renoir’s Portrait of Gabrielle in Red, and two paintings by Camille Pissarro: Factory Near Pontoise and Portrait of Eugene Murer. The gallery also explores the movement’s evolution through Neo-Impressionist works by Maximilien Luce and Belgian painter Théo van Rysselberghe, whose distinctive pointillist technique brought a new scientific approach to color and light. Whether you’re discovering Impressionism for the first time or revisiting familiar favorites, this gallery offers an unforgettable look at the artists who forever changed the way we see the world.
artworks.placeNote: Where the museum’s floor map puts it.

artworks.title: 19th-Century French Gallery
artworks.description: Explore a century of artistic change in the 19th-Century French Gallery, where tradition meets innovation. During the early 1800s, artists followed the strict standards of the Paris Salon and the École des Beaux-Arts, creating polished works inspired by classical ideals. As the century progressed, however, painters began to break away from these conventions, embracing emotion, realism, and new ways of seeing the world. The gallery traces this remarkable evolution, from the dramatic Romanticism of Eugène Delacroix and the refined classicism of Jean-Auguste-Dominique Ingres to the groundbreaking ideas that paved the way for Impressionism. Along the way, artists experimented with bold color, expressive brushwork, and scenes from everyday life, forever changing the course of art history. Highlights include works by renowned artists such as William-Adolphe Bouguereau, Jean-Baptiste-Camille Corot, Gustave Courbet, Théodore Géricault, Jean-Léon Gérôme, Adolphe Jourdan, and Jean-François Millet. Together, these paintings tell the story of a period when artists challenged convention, responded to a rapidly changing world, and redefined what art could be.
artworks.placeNote: Where the museum’s floor map puts it.

artworks.title: Dutch and Flemish Galleries
artworks.description: Journey into the Dutch Golden Age in this gallery of exceptional 16th- and 17th-century Dutch and Flemish art. Featuring some of the finest paintings of their kind in North America, the collection reveals how prosperity, trade, and culture transformed two great European cities—Antwerp and Amsterdam—into centers of artistic innovation. Marvel at Triptych with the Crucifixion, painted between 1518 and 1520 by Goswijn van der Weyden, the oldest work in the museum’s collection and a masterpiece commissioned for a wealthy Catholic patron. As you continue through the gallery, discover how art evolved alongside a growing middle class, with paintings created not only for churches and palaces but also for homes and businesses. Highlights include a striking self-portrait by Ferdinand Bol, Rembrandt’s most accomplished pupil, an expansive landscape by Jacob van Ruisdael, one of Holland’s greatest landscape painters, and works by Samuel van Hoogstraten, Jacob Jordaens, and Willem van de Velde the Younger. Together, these remarkable paintings offer a window into everyday life, faith, commerce, and artistic achievement during one of Europe’s most influential periods.
artworks.placeNote: Where the museum’s floor map puts it.

artworks.title: The Janee Armstrong Friedmann Gallery of French 18th-Century Art
artworks.description: Step into the elegance of 18th-century France in the Friedmann Gallery of French Art, one of the D’Amour Museum of Fine Arts’ most richly decorated spaces. Inspired by the Rococo style, the gallery is filled with graceful curves, playful details, and a sense of lightness that defined the art and design of the period. Discover works by celebrated artists including François Boucher and Jean-Baptiste LePrince, whose paintings capture the romance, leisure, and refined lifestyles of the French aristocracy. Don’t miss Jean-Siméon Chardin’s acclaimed still life Refreshments (1764), a masterful work inspired by Dutch painting traditions, or Jacques Dumont’s Portrait of a Married Couple (1733), which reflects the growing appreciation for individuality and personality in 18th-century portraiture. As you explore, you’ll also see how artistic tastes shifted from the playful elegance of Rococo to the order and balance of Neoclassicism. Influenced by the ideals of ancient Greece and Rome and the spirit of the French Revolution, this later style is represented by Portrait of Madame Servan, in which the sitter wears a gown inspired by the flowing drapery of a classical toga. From lavish interiors to revolutionary ideas, the Friedmann Gallery offers a fascinating journey through one of Europe’s most transformative artistic periods.
artworks.placeNote: Where the museum’s floor map puts it.

artworks.title: In Nature’s Studio: Two Centuries of American Landscape Painting
artworks.description: In Nature’s Studio spotlights the beauty of the American landscape from the early nineteenth century through the late twentieth century. This stunning exhibition combines early depictions of bucolic North American vistas—intimate forest interiors, sweeping panoramic views of natural wonders, and dramatic images of the untamed land and sea—with scenes of Europe, the Near East, and South America. The show begins with an exploration of the emergence of the Hudson River School of painting in the 1830s and 40s. Considered America’s first self-originated movement, the painters of this loosely organized group recorded the natural beauty of the Hudson River Valley in New York, picturesque sites in the Mid-Atlantic, and majestic views of the American West. These artists harnessed the optimism of the young nation and the seemingly endless potential of the American landscape. In addition to works by nineteenth-century landscape artists such as Thomas Birch, Frederic Church, Jasper Francis Cropsey, Worthington Whittredge, William Trost Richards, Hermann Herzog, and Aaron Draper Shattuck, the exhibition also examines the late-nineteenth century shift to Impressionism and Tonalism at the turn of the century by painters including George Inness, N. C. Wyeth, Childe Hassam, Edward Willis Redfield, John Fulton Folinsbee, John Mulhaupt and Robert Spencer. These movements capture the fleeting effects of light and atmosphere by employing new and innovative techniques, including painting outdoors,

artworks.title: Who-ville
artworks.description: Celebrate the holiday spirit all year and discover the story behind one of Dr. Seuss’s most beloved creations in Who-ville, a festive gallery inspired by How the Grinch Stole Christmas! Dr. Seuss often called the Grinch his favorite character, explaining that the story helped him rediscover the meaning of Christmas. Visitors can explore the world of Who-ville with life-size figures of the Grinch and Max, the Who’s beautifully decorated fireplace, and hands-on activities that bring the story to life. Create colorful designs and messages with the giant Light Bright and Pixel Pegs, or help the Grinch travel from Mount Crumpit to Who-ville using a magnetic ball wall filled with ramps, spinners, and tubes. It’s a playful experience where visitors can rediscover the joy, imagination, and heart of a holiday classic.
artworks.placeNote: Where the museum’s floor map puts it.

artworks.title: Young Ted in Springfield
artworks.description: This interactive gallery brings Dr. Seuss’s Springfield childhood to life, exploring the places, family stories, and experiences that helped shape the imagination of one of the world’s most beloved storytellers. Visitors can explore a recreation of Ted’s childhood home at 74 Fairfield Street, where young Ted famously drew on his bedroom walls—and where his mother encouraged his creativity. Try your hand at creating your own whimsical drawings on a digital version of his bedroom walls. Continue the adventure through the places and experiences that inspired Ted’s imagination. Play baker in the Seuss Bakery, inspired by his grandparents’ Howard Street bakery; go fishing at McElligot’s Pool while learning about Ted’s childhood fishing trips with his father; explore the gears and gadgets of the Moose Juice and Goose Juice Brewery, inspired by his family’s Springfield brewing history; and imagine new creatures at the Forest Park Zoo, where Ted’s father served as superintendent and inspired If I Ran the Zoo. Filled with hands-on activities, storytelling, and connections to Springfield history, this gallery invites visitors to experience the city that helped shape Dr. Seuss’s extraordinary imagination.
artworks.placeNote: Where the museum’s floor map puts it.

artworks.title: Fairfield Street
artworks.description: Discover the Springfield that shaped Dr. Seuss in this immersive look at his childhood home, neighborhood, and early inspirations. At the heart of the exhibit is 74 Fairfield Street, the house where Theodor “Ted” Geisel spent his formative years, from age two until he left for college at Dartmouth. Explore a recreation of the Fairfield Street neighborhood and imagine the sights and sounds that surrounded young Ted. Ring the doorbell of the Geisel family home, hear the familiar sounds of the city streets—including trolleys and horse hooves—and discover the places that sparked his curiosity and imagination. Nearby landmarks from Ted’s childhood come to life, including the castle-like Howard Street Armory across from his birthplace and the Barney Mausoleum in Forest Park, with its distinctive sphinx statue and winding stairs. Interactive elements bring the past to life with the sounds of Springfield, including animals from the Forest Park Zoo, where Ted could hear lions roaring from his bedroom at night. This exhibit invites visitors to walk through the Springfield that inspired one of the world’s most beloved storytellers.
artworks.placeNote: Where the museum’s floor map puts it.

artworks.title: The Cat's Corner
artworks.description: The Cat’s Corner Explore, create, and imagine in Cat’s Corner, a playful space where stories and art come together. Curl up with a favorite book, including original stories by Ted Geisel (Dr. Seuss), or join hands-on activities that inspire creativity and build literacy skills. Through art-making, storytelling, and guided activities, children can expand their vocabulary, strengthen reading skills, and bring their own ideas to life through original creations. Designed to support a love of reading and creative expression, Cat’s Corner invites young visitors to discover that every story can inspire something new.

artworks.title: Entry Hall
artworks.description: Begin your journey through the Amazing World of Dr. Seuss Museum with a colorful celebration of Theodor Geisel’s extraordinary career. A larger-than-life mural highlights the evolution of his imagination—from his first children’s book, And to Think That I Saw It on Mulberry Street (1937), to his final book, Oh, the Places You’ll Go! (1991). Bring the story of Springfield to life by sitting on a motorcycle alongside a Mulberry Street police officer—an homage to the Indian Motocycles that may have inspired the motorcycles featured in Geisel’s early work. Look up to discover a whimsical Seuss-inspired glass chandelier, created by artist Dave Colton, featuring vibrant colors and playful trumpet shapes. This welcoming entry space sets the stage for an adventure filled with creativity, curiosity, and the unmistakable imagination of Dr. Seuss. artworks.title: The Amazing World of Dr. Seuss Museum
artworks.description: Discover the imagination and creativity of Springfield native Theodor Geisel—better known as Dr. Seuss! The Amazing World of Dr. Seuss Museum brings his stories, characters, and lifelong connection to Springfield to life through interactive experiences for visitors of all ages. The fully bilingual (English and Spanish) first floor invites families to play with words, explore rhymes, create stories, and discover how Geisel changed the way children learn to read. Upstairs, explore a recreation of his studio and living room featuring his actual furniture and art materials, along with never-before-seen artwork, family photographs, letters, and beloved personal objects, including his childhood stuffed dog, Theophrastus. artworks.title: Readingville
artworks.description: Enter Readingville, where the imagination of Dr. Seuss comes alive through beloved stories, playful challenges, and interactive experiences that celebrate the joy of reading. Explore the world of words at the larger-than-life ABC Wall, inspired by Dr. Seuss’s ABC, where visitors can discover letter sounds, artwork, and vocabulary in a fun, hands-on way. Step into the railroad cave from Green Eggs and Ham to play rhyming games designed for emerging readers, word lovers, and seasoned storytellers alike. Bring favorite stories to life as you climb aboard the Wump of Gump from One Fish Two Fish Red Fish Blue Fish, build towering turtle creations inspired by Yertle the Turtle, and explore the colorful worlds of The Lorax and Horton Hears a Who! with interactive characters and sound experiences. The adventure continues with The Cat in the Hat, where visitors can meet the iconic character that launched generations of readers into the imaginative world of Dr. Seuss. Interactive features invite children and families to play, explore, and create their own Seuss-inspired stories. In Readingville, every corner encourages curiosity, creativity, and a lifelong love of reading.
artworks.placeNote: Where the museum’s floor map puts it.

artworks.title: Ted2Ted
artworks.description: Discover the personal side of Dr. Seuss through a collection of family treasures, memories, and stories that reveal the person behind the beloved books. Explore rare family photographs and a remarkable collection of illustrated letters exchanged between Theodor “Ted” Geisel and his grandnephew, Ted Owens, offering a glimpse into their lifelong relationship and Geisel’s playful creativity. Visitors can also see personal items from Geisel’s childhood, including his favorite chair and cowboy boots, along with a family tree tracing the Seuss and Geisel families. This intimate exhibit invites you to look beyond the characters and discover the family, experiences, and imagination that helped shape the extraordinary life of Dr. Seuss.
artworks.placeNote: Where the museum’s floor map puts it.

artworks.title: Sal da Who: The Making of the Dr. Seuss Sculpture Garden
artworks.description: Discover how the beloved Dr. Seuss National Memorial Sculpture Garden came to life in this behind-the-scenes look at the creative process of artist Lark Grey Dimond-Cates, Dr. Seuss’s stepdaughter and the garden’s creator. Explore bronze maquettes and learn how early designs were transformed into the larger-than-life sculptures that celebrate Theodor Geisel’s imagination and legacy. The display highlights the many stages of creating the garden, including the full-size sculpture of Geisel himself—with hands crafted from casts of his own artistic hands. This unique exhibit offers a glimpse into the artistry, inspiration, and personal connection behind one of Springfield’s most treasured tributes to Dr. Seuss.

artworks.title: Ted, Dr. Seuss
artworks.description: Step into the creative world of Theodor Geisel, a.ka. Dr. Seuss, in a recreation of his La Jolla, California studio and sitting room, filled with the furniture, tools, and personal objects that surrounded him as he brought his imaginative worlds to life. See the chair, drawing table, and art materials Geisel actually used, along with the beloved Geisel Grove sign that once hung in Forest Park while his father served as Superintendent of Parks. Look closely and you may spot Theophrastus, the toy dog gifted to Ted Geisel during his childhood in Springfield that remained a treasured companion throughout his life. The exhibit also features rarely seen artwork and personal notes shared with his stepdaughter, offering a playful and intimate glimpse into the creativity, humor, and personality behind one of the world’s most beloved storytellers.
artworks.placeNote: Where the museum’s floor map puts it.

artworks.title: Lyman & Merrie Wood Museum of Springfield History
artworks.description: Discover the stories, innovations, and people that shaped Springfield and the Connecticut River Valley at the Lyman and Merrie Wood Museum of Springfield History. Through engaging exhibitions, remarkable collections, and interactive experiences, the museum brings the region’s rich past to life for visitors of all ages. Explore Springfield’s legacy as a center of invention and industry through world-renowned collections. See the largest collection of Indian Motorcycles and memorabilia in the world, discover an extraordinary firearms collection featuring the world’s largest collection of Smith & Wesson firearms, and admire beautifully restored automobiles—from an 1899 Knox and a 1901 Crestmobile to elegant Rolls-Royce roadsters from the 1920s. With rotating exhibitions, family-friendly programs, and fascinating stories around every corner, the Wood Museum offers something new to discover with every visit, connecting the history of our region to the innovations that continue to shape the world today. artworks.title: Automobile Gallery
artworks.description: Discover Springfield’s remarkable role in the birth of the American automobile in the Automobile Collection, where historic vehicles reveal the innovation, craftsmanship, and ingenuity that put the city at the forefront of early automotive history. From the first successful gasoline-powered automobile built in the United States to elegant luxury cars of the 20th century, this collection showcases the visionaries and manufacturers who transformed the way people traveled. Duryea In 1893, brothers Charles and Frank Duryea made history when they successfully tested one of the nation’s first gasoline-powered automobiles on the streets of Springfield. The Duryea on display is an exact replica built from the original 1893 plans, representing a groundbreaking moment in American transportation. Stevens-Duryea The success of the Duryea brothers’ invention led to the creation of the Stevens-Duryea Company in 1902, which produced some of America’s most innovative automobiles—including the first six-cylinder engine marketed in the United States. The collection features a privately owned 1911 Model AA, showcasing the company’s reputation for quality and engineering excellence. Knox Automobile Company Springfield inventor Harry Knox helped shape early automobile design with his innovative air-cooled, tiller-steered vehicles. The collection includes an extraordinary 1899 three-wheeled Knox—one of the company’s earliest automobiles—as well as a 1904 Knox Touraine, highlighting Springfield’s p

artworks.title: Made in the Valley
artworks.description: Explore the remarkable story of invention, industry, and ingenuity in Made in the Valley, an exhibit celebrating the products, companies, and creative minds that helped transform Western Massachusetts into a powerhouse of American manufacturing. Beginning around 1800, the Connecticut River Valley became a center of the Industrial Revolution, with Springfield and the surrounding region emerging as one of the nation’s leading manufacturing hubs. From stoves and tools to games, radios, and everyday household products, innovations created here reached homes across the country and reflected the talent and imagination of the people who lived and worked in the region. Discover the stories behind pioneering companies such as Milton Bradley, Merriam-Webster, W.F. Young Company, and Breck, and learn how their ideas, inventions, and craftsmanship left a lasting mark on American life. Made in the Valley celebrates the creativity that has long defined Western Massachusetts—and the innovations that continue to inspire generations. Videos
artworks.placeNote: Where the museum’s floor map puts it.

artworks.title: Springfield History Library & Archives
artworks.description: By Appointment: Tuesday-Friday (Call 413-314-6430) Drop-in Hours: Every Wednesday & First Saturday of the month, 11 am-4 pm Free with museum admission; Library Only: $9 Uncover the stories of the past and explore your own family history at the Springfield History Library and Archives, a valuable resource for researchers, genealogists, and anyone curious about the people and events that shaped our region. Visitors from across the United States and Canada turn to the library’s extensive collections to trace family connections, research local history, and discover stories hidden within generations of records. The archives include a significant collection of French Canadian records, Ellis Island passenger record indexes, the Loiselle Index, more than 20,000 genealogy books, 6,000 microforms, 25,000 photographs, and more than 1.3 million archival documents. From diaries and deeds to account books, land records, photographs, and personal papers, these collections provide a window into the lives of those who came before us. Whether you’re beginning your family history journey or conducting in-depth research, the Springfield History Library and Archives offers the tools and resources to help bring the past to life. artworks.title: Hasbro GameLand
artworks.description: Put your skills to the test in Hasbro GameLand, a hands-on exhibit where visitors can explore the fun of memory, chance, speed, imagination, strategy, and word play. Inspired by the beloved games created by the Milton Bradley Company, this colorful, interactive experience invites visitors to spin, race, build words, solve challenges, and discover new ways to play. Try your luck with an oversized spinner inspired by THE GAME OF LIFE, test your coordination on wobbly balance disks, or compete in a pedal-powered race inspired by the classic game MOUSETRAP. At the Word Play Station, visitors can search for words in English or Spanish on a large interactive screen, explore letter sounds in the Word Nook, and create their own words using oversized letter cubes. The Memory Station challenges players to remember and repeat patterns of flashing lights, while the Imagination Station brings early animation to life with a giant zoetrope—an invention that Milton Bradley helped introduce to American audiences. The exhibit also tells the story of Milton Bradley, who moved to Springfield in 1856 and transformed his printing business into a nationally recognized game company after creating THE CHECKERED GAME OF LIFE, launching the board game industry in America. Explore a timeline of the company’s most popular creations, including CANDY LAND, CHUTES & LADDERS, and TWISTER, and discover how games have brought generations of families together. Whether you’re a longtime fan of classic games or d

artworks.title: Downtown Retail Gallery
artworks.description: Step back into the bustling world of Springfield’s retail history and discover the stores that made the city the premier shopping destination in Western Massachusetts. This exhibition explores the department stores, specialty shops, and local businesses that shaped the shopping experience from the late 19th through early 20th centuries. Through historic photographs, advertisements, memorabilia, and artifacts, visitors can revisit the energy and excitement of downtown Springfield’s thriving retail scene. Explore the stories behind beloved businesses such as D. H. Brigham, Haynes & Company, Forbes & Wallace, Steiger’s, and Johnson’s Bookstore, and discover how these iconic stores became important gathering places for generations of shoppers. More than a look at what people bought, this exhibition reveals how shopping reflected the changing lifestyles, traditions, and community connections of Springfield’s past.

artworks.title: Smith & Wesson Gallery of Firearms History
artworks.description: Explore the history of American innovation through one of Springfield’s most influential industries in Arms Makers of America. This expansive gallery traces the evolution of firearms manufacturing from the American Revolution to the present, revealing how the quest for precision transformed not only weapon design but American industry itself. Discover more than 150 historic firearms, including rare examples produced by the United States Armory at Springfield and Smith & Wesson, two institutions whose groundbreaking manufacturing techniques helped shape the Industrial Revolution. Along the way, vibrant murals, authentic tools, and fascinating artifacts bring the story to life, showing how advances in firearms production led to innovations that influenced countless other industries. Highlights include rare 18th-century muskets, one of the earliest firearms produced by Smith & Wesson, Civil War-era weapons, beautifully engraved Tiffany & Co. presentation pistols, World War I and World War II rifles, Olympic target pistols, and an exquisitely engraved .357 Magnum once displayed in the Smith & Wesson showroom. Whether you’re interested in history, engineering, craftsmanship, or Springfield’s role in shaping American manufacturing, this exhibition offers a fascinating look at the inventions and ideas that changed the nation.

artworks.title: John Brown, Abraham Lincoln and the Civil War
artworks.description: Discover the Springfield story of John Brown, the passionate abolitionist whose years in the city helped shape his commitment to ending slavery and set the stage for one of the most dramatic events in American history. This exhibition explores Brown’s life in Springfield, his role in the abolitionist movement, and his infamous 1859 raid on Harpers Ferry. Through historic artifacts and personal belongings, visitors gain insight into the man behind the movement—including the challenges, convictions, and choices that defined his legacy. Highlights include Brown’s desk, where he helped hide freedom seekers as part of the Underground Railroad; wood and slate from his fort at Harpers Ferry; the hobnail safe from his Springfield wool business; his rocking chair, clay tobacco pipe, surveyor’s rule, and documents bearing his signature. The exhibition also shares the history of the Free Church of Springfield, an important center of abolitionist activity that was later renamed St. John’s Congregational Church in honor of John Brown. Together, these stories reveal Springfield’s important role in the national struggle over slavery and the pursuit of freedom. Sponsored by Mass Humanities, a state-based affiliate of the National Endowment for the Humanities, and Hampden Savings Foundation, Inc., the charitable foundation of Hampden Bank.

artworks.title: Granville Brothers Aircraft
artworks.description: Soar into Springfield’s aviation history and discover the daring innovation of the Granville Brothers Aircraft in this exhibition celebrating the golden age of air racing. In the late 1920s and early 1930s, brothers Zantford Granville and his siblings Edward, Robert, Thomas, and Mark built some of the fastest airplanes in the world right here in Springfield. Known as the “Gee Bee” aircraft, their sleek and powerful racing planes captured the imagination of pilots and aviation enthusiasts during a thrilling era of flight. See the only Zeta aircraft ever built, along with a three-quarter-scale replica of the legendary Gee Bee Model R-1, the racing plane flown by Jimmy Doolittle to victory in the 1932 Thompson Trophy race. The exhibit also features historic trophies, aviation artifacts, photographs, pilot memorabilia, and stories of aviation pioneers including Lowell Bayles, Jimmy Doolittle, Russell Boardman, and Maude Tait. Experience the innovation, ambition, and adventure that made the Granville Brothers—and their remarkable airplanes—a lasting part of Springfield’s place in aviation history.
artworks.galleryName: Gee Bee Aviation: the Granville Brothers’ racing planes

artworks.title: The Esta Manthos Indian Motocycle Collection
artworks.description: Experience the story of one of America’s most iconic motorcycle brands in the Indian Motocycle Collection, home to the largest collection of Indian Motocycles and memorabilia in the world. Founded in Springfield in 1901, Indian Motocycle became a symbol of innovation, speed, and adventure. This remarkable collection showcases more than two dozen historic motocycles alongside photographs, artifacts, and memorabilia that trace the company’s rise from a local startup to a globally recognized manufacturer. See some of the rarest and most significant Indian Motocycles ever built, including a 1904 model personally designed and owned by co-founder Carl Oscar Hedstrom, a 1912 board track racing motocycle with its original racing tires, a beautifully restored 1929 101 Scout, and a rugged 1927 hill-climber. Along the way, discover the stories of the riders, racers, inventors, and workers who helped make Indian Motocycle a Springfield legend. From the company’s early days at the famous “Wigwam” factory to its contributions during times of war and its lasting influence on American motoring culture, this exhibition offers an unforgettable journey through more than half a century of ingenuity, craftsmanship, and Springfield history. Charles Manthos and his Prototype Indian Motocycle Discover the inspiring story of Charlie Manthos, whose passion for Indian Motocycle helped preserve one of Springfield’s greatest legacies.
